route.text: Extend the denominator (Liouville) route of variant-1629563f from one divisibility chain to unions of several. For A a union of chains c_1, ..., c_r, the common denominator of the partial sum below m is the product of 2^(P_i(m)) - 1, where P_i(m) is the largest element of chain i below m, so the criterion applies as soon as the margin m - P_1(m) - ... - P_r(m) is unbounded along elements m of A.

Soc. (N.S.) 12 (1948), 63–66, Theorem (`f(1/t)` irrational for every integer `|t| > 1`; here
`t = 2`). The `n = 0` term is `1/0 = 0` in Lean, so the sum is the sum over `n ≥ 1`. -/

  sorry

/-- Erdős 257 for every infinite arithmetic progression `A = {a + d n : n ≥ 0}` (`d ≥ 1`).
Known: for `a = 0` this is Erdős 1948 at base `t = 2^d` (J. Indian Math. Soc. 12, 63–66,
Theorem); for `a ≥ 1`, `1/(2^(a+dn) - 1) = 2^(-a)/(t^n + q)` with `t = 2^d` and `q = -2^(-a)`, so
it follows from P. B. Borwein, *On the irrationality of ∑ 1/(q^n + r)*, J. Number Theory 37
(1991), 253–259: `∑_{n ≥ 1} 1/(t^n + q)` is irrational for every integer `t ≥ 2` and rational
`q ∉ {0, -t^n}` (as stated by Kovač–Tao, arXiv:2406.17593, §2.1.2). The even and the odd
integers are the cases `d = 2`. A `0` in `A` contributes `1/0 = 0` in Lean. -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_arithmetic_progressions :
    ∀ a d : ℕ, 0 < d →
      Irrational (∑' m : {m : ℕ | ∃ n, m = a + d * n}, (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ m.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős 257 for every infinite `A` whose indicator is eventually periodic (for example any
arithmetic progression, the odd numbers, any union of residue classes, changed in finitely many
places). Known: F. Luca and Y. Tachiya, *Irrationality of Lambert series associated with a
periodic sequence*, Int. J. Number Theory 10 (2014), 623–636, Theorem 1.1 (restated as Theorem A,
RIMS Kôkyûroku 2014 (2017), p. 139): `∑ a(n)/(q^n - 1)` is irrational for every purely periodic
integer sequence `a`, not identically zero, and every integer `|q| > 1`. An eventually periodic
infinite `A` differs from a nonempty purely periodic set in finitely many places, which changes
the sum by a rational number. -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_eventually_periodic :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, A.Infinite →
      (∃ p N : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∀ n, N ≤ n → (n ∈ A ↔ n + p ∈ A)) →
      Irrational (∑' n : A, (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős 257 for sets that are eventually lacunary of ratio two: if `A` is an infinite set of
positive integers and, from some point `N` on, any two elements `n < m` of `A` satisfy `m ≥ 2n`,
then `∑_{n ∈ A} 1/(2^n - 1)` is irrational. Examples: `{2^k}`, `{2^k - 1}`, `{3^k}`, `{k!}`, any
infinite divisibility chain, and any finite set joined to one of these.

Proof by Liouville's criterion (`Opn.erdos_257_liouville_criterion`): finitely many terms change
the sum by a rational, so assume the ratio condition for all pairs. Call `a ∈ A` non-doubling
when `2a ∉ A`. If infinitely many elements are non-doubling, then for `m ∈ A` the elements below
`m` sum to at most `m` minus the number of non-doubling ones among them (induction on the
largest), so the product of their `2^a - 1` is at most `2^(m - C)` once `C` non-doubling elements
lie below `m`. If finitely many are, all below `b`, then above `b` the set is a doubling chain,
every element of `A` from `b` to `n` divides `n`, and with `m = 2n` the common denominator
`(∏_{a ∈ A, a ≤ b} (2^a - 1)) · (2^n - 1)` is at most `2^(m - C)` for `n` large. Either way the
positive tail from `m` on, below `4 · 2^(-m)`, cannot be a positive multiple of `1/(qL)`.

Covered in principle by Erdős (Math. Student 36, 1968), who proves irrationality for pairwise
coprime `A` with summable reciprocals and remarks that coprimality can be dropped; ratio
below two is beyond this elementary argument. -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_eventually_ratio_two :
    ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.Infinite → 0 ∉ A →
    (∃ N : ℕ, ∀ m ∈ A, ∀ n ∈ A, N ≤ n → n < m → 2 * n ≤ m) →
    Irrational (∑' n : A, (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

import Mathlib

/-- Liouville's criterion for Erdős 257: let `A` be an infinite set of positive integers such
that, for every `C`, some `m ∈ A` has a common multiple `L` of the numbers `2^a - 1` over the
elements `a < m` of `A` with `2^C · L ≤ 2^m` (the elements below `m` have a small common
denominator compared with the gap the tail leaves). Then `∑_{n ∈ A} 1/(2^n - 1)` is irrational.
Proof: if the sum were `p/q`, take `C` with `2^C > 4q`; with `L` as above, `q · L` times the tail
from `m` on is a positive integer, but the tail is below `4 · 2^(-m)`, so it is below
`4q · 2^(-C) < 1`. The criterion covers every set that is eventually lacunary of ratio two
(`Opn.erdos_257_eventually_ratio_two`: `{2^k}`, `{2^k - 1}`, `{3^k}`, `{k!}`, divisibility
chains). It does not reach sets of positive density, nor lacunary sets of ratio below two in
general; those need Erdős's arguments (1948, 1968). -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_liouville_criterion :
    ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.Infinite → 0 ∉ A →
    (∀ C : ℕ, ∃ m ∈ A, ∃ L : ℕ, 0 < L ∧ (∀ a ∈ A, a < m → 2 ^ a - 1 ∣ L) ∧ 2 ^ C * L ≤ 2 ^ m) →
    Irrational (∑' n : A, (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

import Mathlib
import Nodes.«variant-41d1f19b».Context

/-- Erdős 257 for sets with arbitrarily long gaps: let `A` be an infinite set of positive
integers such that, for every `C`, some `m ∈ A` exceeds the sum of all elements of `A` below it
by at least `C`. Then `∑_{n ∈ A} 1/(2^n - 1)` is irrational.

The hypothesis allows long dense blocks between the gaps, so the reciprocal sum `∑_{n ∈ A} 1/n`
may diverge: for `A = ⋃_j [X_j, 2X_j]` with `X_{j+1} = 4X_j^2` each block contributes more than
`1/2` to it, while the elements below `X_{j+1}` sum to less than `3X_j^2`. Such sets are covered
neither by Erdős (Math. Student 36, 1968), whose sets have summable reciprocals, nor by the
periodic and multiplicative cases listed in the literature record.

Proof (Liouville's criterion, `Opn.erdos_257_liouville_criterion`, with the product of the
`2^a - 1` over the elements below `m` as the common denominator, which is at most
`2^(m - C)`). -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_long_gaps :
    ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.Infinite → 0 ∉ A →
    (∀ C : ℕ, ∃ m ∈ A, ∃ F : Finset ℕ, (∀ a, a ∈ F ↔ a ∈ A ∧ a < m) ∧ C + ∑ a ∈ F, a ≤ m) →
    Irrational (∑' n : A, (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

import Mathlib
import Nodes.«variant-037e597d».Context

/-- Erdős 257 for the powers of two together with the powers of three:
`∑_{n ∈ {2^k} ∪ {3^k}} 1/(2^n - 1)` is irrational. The set is not lacunary of ratio two
(`2^k < 3^j < 2^(k+1)` happens infinitely often), so `Opn.erdos_257_eventually_ratio_two` does
not apply, but Liouville's criterion (`Opn.erdos_257_liouville_criterion`) does. Each part is a
divisibility chain, so below `m` the common denominator of the partial sum is
`(2^(2^k) - 1)(2^(3^J) - 1)`, with `2^k` and `3^J` the largest powers below `m`; taking
`m = min(2^(k+1), 3^(J+1))`, it suffices that some power `2^k` lies in `[3^J + C, 2·3^J - C]`.
If that failed for both `J` and `J + 1`, both `3^J` and `3^(J+1)` would lie within `C` of a power
of two, `2^x` and `2^y`, and then `|2^y - 3·2^x| < 4C`. But `|2^y - 3·2^x| ≥ 2^x`, because
`2^d ≠ 3`. That is impossible once `3^J ≥ 5C + 1`. The reciprocals of the set are
summable, so the result is covered in principle by Erdős's remark (Math. Student 36, 1968) that
coprimality can be dropped from his 1968 theorem; the proof here is elementary and complete. -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_powers_of_two_and_three :
    Irrational (∑' n : ({n | ∃ k : ℕ, n = 2 ^ k} ∪ {n | ∃ k : ℕ, n = 3 ^ k} : Set ℕ),
      (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

import Mathlib
import Nodes.«variant-f93b89d8».Context

/-- Erdős 257 for the union of the powers of two integer bases `2 ≤ a < b`:
`∑_{n ∈ {a^k} ∪ {b^k}} 1/(2^n - 1)` is irrational. This generalises
`Opn.erdos_257_powers_of_two_and_three` (the case `a = 2`, `b = 3`) to every pair of bases, with
no independence condition on `a` and `b`. Each part is a divisibility chain, so below `m` the
partial sum has the common denominator `(2^(a^J) - 1)(2^(b^K) - 1)`, where `a^J` and `b^K` are
the largest powers below `m`, and Liouville's criterion (`Opn.erdos_257_liouville_criterion`)
applies once `m - a^J - b^K` is unbounded along such `m`. Put `Z = b^(K+1)` and let `a^J` be the
largest power of `a` with `a^J ≤ Z`. Either `m = Z` has margin `Z - b^K - a^J ≥ C`, or `a^J` lies
within `b^K + C` of `Z`; in that case `m = a^(J+1)` (when `a ≥ 3`) or `m = 2^(J+2)` (when `a = 2`
and `b ≥ 4`) has margin at least `2 b^K - 2C`. Only the pair `(2, 3)` needs more: there the
Diophantine step `|2^y - 3·2^x| ≥ 2^x` from the proof of the two-and-three case is used. The
proof is elementary and complete. -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_powers_of_two_bases :
    ∀ a b : ℕ, 2 ≤ a → a < b →
    Irrational (∑' n : ({n | ∃ k : ℕ, n = a ^ k} ∪ {n | ∃ k : ℕ, n = b ^ k} : Set ℕ),
      (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

import Mathlib
import Nodes.«variant-77c0756e».Context

/-- Erdős 257 for the union of two fast divisibility chains. Let `x` and `y` be sequences of
positive integers in which each term divides the next and is at most a third of it
(`x j ∣ x (j+1)` and `3 x j ≤ x (j+1)`, the same for `y`). Then
`∑_{n ∈ range x ∪ range y} 1/(2^n - 1)` is irrational. Examples: the powers of any two bases
`a, b ≥ 3`, or `{3^k} ∪ {(3k)!}`, or `{2·3^k} ∪ {5^k}`. Such a union need not be lacunary of
ratio two, and the elements below an element need not sum to less than it, so neither
`Opn.erdos_257_eventually_ratio_two` nor `Opn.erdos_257_long_gaps` applies. The proof uses
Liouville's criterion (`Opn.erdos_257_liouville_criterion`): below `m` the partial sum has the
common denominator `(2^(x J) - 1)(2^(y K) - 1)`, with `x J` and `y K` the largest chain elements
below `m`. Put `Z = y (K+1)` and let `x J` be the largest `x`-element with `x J ≤ Z`. Either
`m = Z` leaves margin `Z - y K - x J ≥ C`, or `x J > Z - y K - C`, and then
`m = min (x (J+1)) (y (K+2))` leaves margin at least `C`, because `x (J+1) ≥ 3 x J` and
`Z ≥ 3 y K`. The proof is elementary and complete. -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_two_chains :
    ∀ x y : ℕ → ℕ, 0 < x 0 → 0 < y 0 →
    (∀ j, x j ∣ x (j + 1)) → (∀ j, y j ∣ y (j + 1)) →
    (∀ j, 3 * x j ≤ x (j + 1)) → (∀ j, 3 * y j ≤ y (j + 1)) →
    Irrational (∑' n : (Set.range x ∪ Set.range y : Set ℕ), (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by

/-- Erdős 257 for a union of finitely many lacunary sequences. Let `c 0, …, c (r-1)` be `r ≥ 1`
sequences of positive integers, each growing by a factor of at least `(2r+1)^(r+1)` from one
term to the next (no divisibility and no relation between the sequences is assumed). Then
`∑_{n ∈ A} 1/(2^n - 1)` is irrational for `A` the union of their ranges. For `r = 1` the
factor is 9 (a case `Opn.erdos_257_eventually_ratio_two` already covers); for three sequences
it is `7^4 = 2401`, met for instance by `n ↦ 2401^n`, `n ↦ 3·2401^n` and
`n ↦ (n + 1)·2401^n`, the last not a divisibility chain. The union need not be lacunary of ratio two,
so `Opn.erdos_257_eventually_ratio_two` does not apply, and the sequences need not be
divisibility chains, as `Opn.erdos_257_two_chains` requires. Proof: by pigeonhole over the
`r + 1` windows `(q^k T, q^(k+1) T]`, `q = 2r+1`, `k = 0, …, r`, one window contains no
element of `A`, because two elements of one sequence in `(T, q^(r+1) T]` would contradict its
growth. The least element `m` of `A` above `q^k T` then exceeds `(2r+1) q^k T`, while the
elements of each sequence below `m` are at most `q^k T` and sum to at most twice that. So `m`
exceeds the sum of all smaller elements of `A` by at least `T`, and Liouville's criterion
(`Opn.erdos_257_liouville_criterion`, common denominator `∏_{a ∈ A, a < m} (2^a - 1)`)
applies, as in `Opn.erdos_257_long_gaps`. The proof is elementary and complete. -/
theorem Opn.erdos_257_lacunary_union :
    ∀ (r : ℕ) (c : Fin r → ℕ → ℕ), 0 < r → (∀ i, 0 < c i 0) →
    (∀ i j, (2 * r + 1) ^ (r + 1) * c i j ≤ c i (j + 1)) →
    Irrational (∑' n : (⋃ i, Set.range (c i) : Set ℕ), (1 : ℝ) / (2 ^ n.1 - 1)) := by
  sorry

references.note: Theorem (p. 63): f(1/t) = Σ 1/(t^n − 1) is irrational for every integer |t| > 1. Case A = ℕ (t = 2) and, at t = 2^d, A = dℕ.
references.title: P. Erdős, On arithmetical properties of Lambert series, J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) 12 (1948), 63–66

references.note: As stated by Kovač–Tao §2.1.2 p. 4: Σ_{n≥1} 1/(t^n + q) is irrational for integer t ≥ 2 and rational q ∉ {0, −t^n}. Rescaling 1/(2^(a+dn) − 1) = 2^(−a)/(2^(dn) − 2^(−a)) gives every arithmetic progression A.
references.title: P. B. Borwein, On the irrationality of Σ 1/(q^n + r), J. Number Theory 37 (1991), 253–259

references.note: Σ a(n)/(q^n − 1) is irrational for every purely periodic integer sequence a(n), not identically zero, and every integer |q| > 1. With a = 1_A this settles every infinite A whose indicator is eventually periodic (finite changes add a rational): all arithmetic progressions, the odd integers (their Example 2, p. 140), unions of residue classes.
references.title: F. Luca and Y. Tachiya, Irrationality of Lambert series associated with a periodic sequence, Int. J. Number Theory 10 (2014), 623–636, Theorem 1.1 (restated as Theorem A in RIMS Kôkyûroku 2014 (2017), 138–150, p. 139)

references.note: Theorem (p. 222): pairwise coprime n_i with Σ 1/n_i < ∞ give Σ 1/(t^{n_i} − 1) irrational for every t ≥ 2. Erdős says coprimality can be removed 'by more complicated arguments' (no details), that he knows no infinite sequence with a rational sum 'though it seems likely that this can happen', and expects irrationality whenever n_{k+1} − n_k → ∞.
references.title: P. Erdős, On the irrationality of certain series, Math. Student 36 (1968), 222–226

references.note: Corollary 1.2 and Examples 1.1–1.3 (p. 4 of the author preprint at danielduverney.fr): irrational (indeed linearly independent with 1) for A = the squarefree numbers at base 2, A = the perfect k-th powers {n^k} at every base, A = the sums of two squares, A = the integers coprime to N.
references.title: D. Duverney and Y. Tachiya, Refinement of the Chowla–Erdős method and linear independence of certain Lambert series, Forum Math. 31 (2019), 1557–1566

references.note: Proves Σ_p 1/(2^p − 1) = Σ ω(n)/2^n irrational (A = primes; also Erdős #69). The paragraph after it says a similar argument gives every base b ≥ 2 and the prime powers (Σ Ω(n)/2^n) but leaves the details 'to the interested reader': the prime-power case is sketched, not proved.
references.title: T. Tao and J. Teräväinen, Quantitative correlations and some problems on prime factors of consecutive integers, arXiv:2512.01739v2 (Apr 2026), Theorem 1.3 (§1.3, p. 4)

references.note: §2.1.2 pp. 4–5: subset sums are distinct and form a Cantor set 'in the topological sense', so at most countably many counterexamples; 'We do not know how to solve the original question'. Remark 4.1 p. 13: Σ_{l>n} 1/(t^l − 1) < 1/(t^n − 1). Nothing is said about the measure of the subsum set.
references.title: V. Kovač and T. Tao, On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series, arXiv:2406.17593v4; Acta Math. Hungar. 175 (2025), 572–608, §2.1.2 and Remark 4.1

references.note: Thm 2.3: with bases t_1 < … < t_m and Σ 1/(t_k − 1) > 1 a rational mixed sum exists. Thm 2.5: 2^n is not a Type 3 irrationality sequence, i.e. Σ 1/(2^n + b_n) is rational for some bounded nonzero integers b_n, disproving Erdős's 1988 perturbed speculation.
references.title: V. Kovač and T. Tao, On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series, arXiv:2406.17593v4; Acta Math. Hungar. 175 (2025), 572–608, Theorems 2.3 and 2.5

references.note: If every term exceeds its tail, the subsum set is a Cantor set of Lebesgue measure lim 2^k X_k (credited to Hornich 1941). For x_n = 1/(2^n − 1), 2^k X_k = Σ_{j≥1} 1/(2^j − 2^(−k)) decreases to 1, so the subsum set has measure exactly 1 inside [0, 1.6067…]: this is the precise form of Kovač's 'fat Cantor set'.
references.title: Z. Nitecki, Subsum sets: intervals, Cantor sets, and Cantorvals, arXiv:1106.3779v2 (2013), Theorem 4(1), p. 9

references.note: p. 105: asks whether Σ 1/(2^{n_k} − 1) is irrational for every sequence, 'or perhaps Σ 1/(2^{n_k} − t_k) … for every |t_k| < C'; p. 102 records Borwein's 1987 announcement.
references.title: P. Erdős, On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results, New Advances in Transcendence Theory (Durham 1986), CUP 1988, 102–109

references.note: Claims Lean proofs (not reviewed here; formal-conjectures links them for erdos_257.variants.tsum_top and .summable_reciprocal_support) of: the coprimality-free reciprocal-summable case at every base; a weighted criterion covering some A with divergent Σ 1/a (Theorem 1); A = ℕ, periodic, residue-class and odd supports; measure of the subsum set = 1 (Theorem 7); membership ⇔ greedy survival (Theorem 10). It states the universal problem remains open.
references.title: W. Cook, Reciprocal Mersenne Subseries (unrefereed, AI-assisted research record with Lean 4.29 corpus), github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos

references.note: Lists the general problem as open (last edited 15 Apr 2026); 0 proof claims.
references.title: T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problem #257, erdosproblems.com

literature_proposed.summary: Open. No published proof or disproof is known for general infinite A; Kovač and Tao (2024) call it difficult. Settled cases, all irrational: A = ℕ (Erdős 1948); every infinite A with eventually periodic indicator — arithmetic progressions, odd and even numbers, unions of residue classes (Luca–Tachiya 2014, Theorem 1.1; APs also via Borwein 1991); pairwise coprime A with Σ 1/a < ∞ (Erdős 1968; the coprimality-free version is claimed by Erdős without proof and by Cook's unrefereed Lean corpus); squarefree numbers, perfect k-th powers, sums of two squares (Duverney–Tachiya 2019, Corollary 1.2); the primes (Tao–Teräväinen, Theorem 1.3). Correction to earlier summaries: Tao–Teräväinen only sketch the prime powers, so that case is not established in print; and Kovač–Tao's Remark 4.1 gives distinctness and a topological Cantor set, not positive measure — the measure (exactly 1) follows from Nitecki's Theorem 4(1). Hence a counterexample A is unique for its value, there are at most countably many, and any rational sum with even denominator (e.g. 1/2) would need an infinite A. Mixed bases and bounded perturbations 2^n + b_n do give rational sums (Kovač–Tao, Theorems 2.3, 2.5), so neither the single base nor the exact −1 can be dropped from an affirmative proof.

justification.text: The divisor is zero only at n = 0, where Lean's junk value makes the term 0; the sum over A then equals the sum over A without 0, which is still infinite, and the informal statement never uses n = 0.
